explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Shem, Ham and Japheth are the three, and from them the whole earth was populated (Genesis 9:19). Three brothers, and the whole earth full of people! I once stamped one batch of cookies and needed a nap. These three had a whole planet to fill.

A city is too small, friend. The verse says these three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth was populated. That's the whole earth, not one city. Picture one family photo that keeps needing a bigger wall.
Close, but a camp is way too small. Genesis 9:19 says that from these three sons, the whole earth was populated. That's no campfire crowd. That's a family that kept growing and growing.

A vineyard, baker! Noah, a man of the soil, plants one, and then he drinks some of its wine (Genesis 9:20-21). I know a thing or two about a batch going sideways. I once left a tray in the oven for one more minute. ONE minute. The text doesn't hide what happened next, and neither will I.

Olive grove! I get it, friend, it sounds so farmer-ish, so very Bible. But the verse says Noah, a man of the soil, planted a vineyard (Genesis 9:20). Verse 21 then mentions its wine, so no olives in this one. Don't worry, I've mixed up a topping before too, and the cookies forgave me.
A wheat field would be a fine thing to plant, I won't argue with that. But that's not what this verse says. Noah planted a vineyard, and verse 21 says he drank some of its wine.

explanations.answer: He tells his two brothers outside
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside. The text says nothing more about what was in his heart, so I won't guess. I think this is a hard moment, so let's move through it carefully.

The text doesn't say that. Noah doesn't wake up until verse 24, after his sons have acted. What Ham does is see his father's nakedness and tell his two brothers outside. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.

The text says Ham didn't keep it to himself. He saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside. I think this is a heavy moment, and I'm not going to add anything the Bible doesn't say about it.

That's it. Shem and Japheth walk in backward and cover their father, with their faces turned away so they don't see his nakedness. Try carrying a garment across your shoulders while walking backward. I'd have knocked over every mixing bowl in the bakery.
The text never mentions waiting or what time of day it was. It tells us how they went in. They walked backward, and their faces were turned away so they did not see their father's nakedness.
Nobody gets sent in this scene. Shem and Japheth take the garment themselves and cover their father. And they do it walking backward, with their faces turned away.
Right. Noah wakes up, learns what his youngest son had done, and says, "Cursed be Canaan!" Canaan is Ham's son, and the text doesn't tell us why Noah names him. So I won't guess at a reason.

That's the name you'd expect, since Ham is the one in the story. But the words Noah speaks are "Cursed be Canaan!" Canaan is Ham's son. The text doesn't give a reason for naming him, so we leave that open too.
Put is a real name in this passage. He's one of Ham's sons, listed in Genesis 10:6 next to Cush, Mizraim and Canaan. But Noah doesn't say his name. The curse he speaks is "Cursed be Canaan!"

True. Noah says, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem!" and then, "May Canaan be the servant of Shem." The two sentences come back to back. Verse 27 goes on to say, "…may Canaan be his servant." and the text doesn't spell out whose servant that is.

It's true, friend, and here's what the text says. Noah declares, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem!" and in the same breath, "May Canaan be the servant of Shem." So Canaan is named as Shem's servant right after the blessing. Verse 27 then says, "…may Canaan be his servant." and it leaves open whose servant that is.

Yes. Noah says, "May God expand the territory of Japheth…" That's a wish for more room, and the words are "may God," so it's what Noah asks for. Every cookie sheet in my bakery is full, so I understand wishing for more space.
Long life is a good thing to wish for, but that's not what Noah says. His words for Japheth are "May God expand the territory of Japheth…" That's about land, not years.
A great name sounds nice, but it isn't in Noah's words here. What Noah says is "May God expand the territory of Japheth…" He's talking about more room.
That's the number. After the flood, Noah lived 350 years. Add that up and the verse after it gives his total: 950 years, and then he died. That's a lot of birthdays for one man.

120 is a good guess, but it isn't the number in this verse. The text says that after the flood, Noah lived 350 years. Together with the years before, that makes 950 in all. That's a lot more than 120.
Forty shows up in Noah's story, but for the rain. The rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights (Genesis 7:12). After the flood, the text says Noah lived 350 years.
